analysis.one_liner: Lets states skip the health plan benefit rules where only one insurer sells coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from January 2017 until Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a state waive the Affordable Care Act's 'essential health benefits' rules if any county in the state has only one health insurer selling individual coverage. In those states, plans sold to individuals and small businesses could leave out required benefits like hospitalization, maternity care, and mental health services for up to five years at a time, renewable. The idea is that in places where one insurer faces no competition, required benefit packages can push premiums so high that people can't afford any coverage at all. Insurers could still sell plans with the full benefit package if they chose to.
analysis.who_benefits: People in one-insurer markets, most prominently Alaska, where every county had a single individual-market insurer at the time, who face premiums inflated by the requirement to cover a full benefit package. Insurers in those states also gain, because they could sell cheaper, stripped-down plans without offering the full package.

how_it_helps.text: In a state with any county served by only one individual-market insurer, the bill lifts the requirement that plans cover the ACA's essential health benefits in the individual and small-group markets and on the exchanges [S2] [S3].
The waiver lasts up to five years and can be renewed as long as the state still has a one-insurer county, and insurers remain free to sell full-benefit plans if they want to [S3].
Plans sold without the full benefit package would still count as coverage under the individual mandate, so someone buying a cheaper plan would not owe the penalty for going uninsured [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who need the mandated benefits most — those expecting hospital stays, maternity care, mental health or prescription drug needs — would find fewer plans covering those services, and plans excluding sick customers could leave the remaining risk pool sicker and pricier.

drawbacks.text: The waiver is triggered by conditions in a single county but strips benefit requirements statewide, so consumers in well-served counties of the same state lose required benefits too [S3].

Removing required benefits can leave people with plans that look cheap until they need hospital care, maternity coverage, or mental health treatment, and thinner coverage can pull healthier people out of plans that do cover those services, raising costs for those who remain — a trade an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: where an insurer has a local monopoly, mandatory benefit packages can price coverage out of reach, and Alaska's single-insurer market was the textbook case. But the remedy is blunt. It strips protections statewide on the strength of one county's problem, and cheaper plans would come at the cost of leaving serious medical needs uncovered. A more tailored fix — regional waivers, or requiring a cheaper full-benefit option instead of allowing bare plans — would have handled the tradeoff better.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and never moved again before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].
On January 25, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action is recorded for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and the benefit-mandate status quo: because the bill died, no state gained the authority to sell plans without the essential health benefits package, and consumers kept the existing coverage requirements unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and the benefit-mandate status quo

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his state's delegation response to a market where only one insurer sold individual coverage statewide

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and its Health Subcommittee for the entire Congress without scheduling a markup or vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan divide ever showed up in a vote [S4].

industries.note: In waiver states, insurers would have gained the option to sell cheaper plans without covering hospitalization, maternity, or mental health care, while the bill also preserved their existing customers' mandate-compliance if they bought such plans. A freer hand on benefits cuts costs but shifts medical needs onto people who buy the stripped-down coverage.
